meta.description: Not Carroll. The line is in none of his books, and Wikiquote traces it to French-language social media. Who wrote it is still unknown.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'But, said Alice, if the world has absolutely no sense, who's stopping us from inventing one?'?
meta.ogDescription: Alice never says it. We searched twelve of Carroll’s works; the phrase is in none of them. Wikiquote points to French social media.

answer.label: Not Lewis Carroll — and Alice never says it
answer.authorDates: Author unestablished · in circulation at least since 2017
answer.sourceLine: Carroll did not write this and Alice does not say it. We searched twelve of his English works end to end — both Alice books included — and the sentence is absent; so is every distinctive piece of it, including the phrases “absolutely no sense”, “stopping us” and “inventing one”. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗ and records that it “originated in French-speaking social media as attributed to Carroll”, citing a 2017 investigation by the writer Clémentine Beauvais. We could not open that post — its host is blocked from this machine — so we pass on Wikiquote’s summary of it and stop there. Who actually wrote the sentence is unknown.

source.heading: What the books actually say

docMeta.dd: Twelve of Carroll’s English books, 2.1 million characters
None — and none of the phrase fragments either

source.excerpt: “But, said Alice, if the world has absolutely no sense, who’s stopping us from inventing one?”
trail: We downloaded the Project Gutenberg texts of twelve of Carroll’s English works — Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, Through the Looking-Glass, Alice’s Adventures Under Ground, The Nursery “Alice”, The Hunting of the Snark, Phantasmagoria and Other Poems, Songs from Alice, Sylvie and Bruno, Sylvie and Bruno Concluded, A Tangled Tale, The Game of Logic and Symbolic Logic — flattened every line break so no phrase could hide across a line ending, and searched 2.1 million characters of it. The full sentence does not occur. Nor does “absolutely no sense”, nor “stopping us”, nor “inventing one” — zero hits each, across all twelve books.

Wikiquote’s page for Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland ↗ lists this line in its Misattributed section with the note that it “originated in French-speaking social media as attributed to Carroll, but no similar passages appear in his written works”. It cites a 2017 post by Clémentine Beauvais ↗ as its reference. That post is hosted on a domain this machine is not permitted to reach, and there is no Wayback capture of it, so we have not read it. The link is here for you; the claim on this page rests on Wikiquote’s summary alone.

We also ran the phrase through a full-text search of the whole of Wikiquote — an insource: query, which reads the raw wikitext of every page on the site — rather than only Carroll’s own page. The phrase “who’s stopping us from inventing one” appears on exactly one page in all of Wikiquote: the Alice page, in the Misattributed list. It is nowhere in Carroll’s own quotation page ↗, in any section.

The tell is in the register. Carroll’s Alice is a literal-minded Victorian child who argues about the meanings of words; she does not propose inventing a world. A line that opens “But, said Alice” — narration in the wrong place, a dialogue tag Carroll would have set off with quotation marks — reads like a sentence translated into English and then attributed backwards, which is consistent with the French trail Wikiquote describes.
source.excerptNote: There is no context to show, because there is no passage to show it from. Alice does complain about sense and nonsense in the real book — the word “nonsense” turns up seven times in Wonderland alone — but never in anything resembling this sentence, and never as a call to invent a better world.

source.rightsNote: No rights badge, deliberately. Carroll’s own writing has been out of copyright for over a century, but this sentence is not Carroll’s, and we could not establish whose it is or when it was written — so there is nothing here whose status we can honestly certify. If it began as a recent social-media post, it would be the poster’s, and in copyright.

author.name: Lewis Carroll
author.heading: About the name on the graphic
author.bio: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson — Lewis Carroll on the title page — taught mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford for most of his adult life, and wrote the two Alice books and a shelf of logic puzzles alongside it. His actual sentences are odd in a specific way: precise, deadpan, and usually about the rules of language rather than about feelings. That is worth knowing, because the lines invented for him are almost always the opposite — warm, motivational, and about you.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a clean case: a modern sentence, pinned on a Victorian book, with no intermediate stage anyone has documented in English.

items.who: Lewis Carroll, in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
items.why: Absent from the complete text of Wonderland ↗, from Through the Looking-Glass ↗, and from ten more of his books we searched. Not one fragment of it occurs.

Wikiquote ↗ states the line “originated in French-speaking social media” and cites Clémentine Beauvais’s 2017 post. We could not open that post to check the evidence behind it, so we report the claim without endorsing its detail.

items.who: “Everyone wants a magical solution to their problem…”
items.why: The entry directly above this one on Wikiquote ↗ is another modern line credited to Alice in Wonderland; Wikiquote traces it to a 2012 episode of the television series Once Upon a Time. Carroll attracts this because everybody recognises the setting and almost nobody has the text to hand.

misattribution.truthLine: The certain part is the negative, and it is checkable in a minute: Wonderland is free to read in full ↗ and this sentence is not in it. The uncertain part — who did write it — we have left open rather than filled in.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is a small philosophical argument wearing a children’s book as a costume: if reality is absurd, absurdity is a licence rather than a defeat. That is a genuinely twentieth-century move — it sounds like Camus in a party dress — and it is the reason the sentence works as a caption and does not work as Victorian prose.

Carroll’s Alice would not have said it because Carroll’s Alice does not think nonsense is liberating. She finds it maddening, and spends both books trying to make the inhabitants of Wonderland follow the rules they keep breaking. The invented line reverses the book’s actual attitude, which is a useful reminder that a misquotation can be popular precisely because it improves on the original’s mood.
context.pull: Carroll’s Alice does not find nonsense liberating. She finds it maddening.
